item.title: JavaScript Promises Logged as Pending Why and How to Fix

“JavaScript Promises Logged as Pending Why and How to Fix”

It’s a common scenario: you execute a function that returns a Promise, perhaps to perform an asynchronous operation like fetching data or logging in a user, and when you try to log the result immediately, you see Promise { <pending> }. This indicates that the Promise hasn’t settled yet – it’s neither resolved nor rejected.

The fundamental reason for this behavior lies in the nature of asynchronous operations and how Promises are designed to manage them. Promises represent the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. The pending state signifies that the operation is still in progress.

item.title: Solved: How to Avoid the Explicit Construction Anti-Pattern in JavaScript Promises
item.description:
“Solved: How to Avoid the Explicit Construction Anti-Pattern in JavaScript Promises”

At its core, the anti-pattern involves creating a new Promise instance and then manually resolving or rejecting it inside a .then() callback of an existing promise. Promises are designed to abstract one-time operations, providing a cleaner way to manage asynchronous operations by making them behave more like synchronous code, without concealing their asynchronous nature.

The Pitfall of Manual Promise Construction

The primary issue with the explicit-construction anti-pattern is its failure to embrace promise chaining. Promises are inherently designed to chain using the .then() method, allowing you to return another promise directly from a .then() callback. This creates a much more elegant and robust asynchronous flow.

item.title: Solved: How to Effectively Manage Async Await with JavaScript Loops
item.description:
“Solved: How to Effectively Manage Async Await with JavaScript Loops”

Why Array.prototype.forEach Fails with Async/Await

The core issue stems from how Array.prototype.forEach is designed. It’s a synchronous iteration method. When you provide an async function as its callback, the callback does return a Promise. However, forEach itself does not wait for this Promise to resolve or reject. It simply fires off the asynchronous call and immediately proceeds to the next iteration. This means all asynchronous operations are initiated in quick succession, but the forEach loop completes its execution long before any of those operations might actually finish.

How Does JavaScript Handle Asynchronous Code, and Why Isn’t My Variable Updated Instantly?

JavaScript operates on a single thread. This implies that only one piece of code can execute at any given moment. However, this single-threaded nature doesn’t mean JavaScript waits idly for long-running operations, such as fetching data from a server, loading an image, or reading a file, to complete. Instead, it employs an asynchronous, non-blocking execution model.

item.title: Efficiently Run Multiple Async Operations in JavaScript
item.description:
“Efficiently Run Multiple Async Operations in JavaScript”

When working with JavaScript’s asynchronous operations, a common requirement is to run several of these tasks concurrently and then execute subsequent code only after all of them have completed. This is crucial for improving performance by avoiding sequential execution where parallelism is possible.

One of the most effective methods for achieving this is by leveraging Promise.all. This built-in JavaScript function accepts an iterable (like an array) of promises and returns a single promise. This returned promise resolves when all of the input promises have resolved, or it rejects as soon as any of the input promises reject. The results are returned in an array, maintaining the original order of the input promises.

This post explores various effective techniques to achieve sequential promise execution, covering modern async/await syntax, traditional Promise chaining, and utility functions.

item.title: JavaScript Loop Index Issue: Capturing Loop Variables in Async Callbacks
item.description:
“JavaScript Loop Index Issue: Capturing Loop Variables in Async Callbacks”

When working with asynchronous operations within JavaScript for loops, a common challenge arises where the loop index variable appears to have its final value in all callbacks. This occurs because a standard for loop in JavaScript executes to completion before its asynchronous operations finish, and callbacks are invoked later. During this interval, the loop index continues to update, so by the time a callback executes, the index variable holds its last assigned value for all pending callbacks.
